clue.text: (& 23ac.) Bugger, say, shaggy cur, Cyclops?

blocks.note: 'bugger' is an example of an angry word, a cross word
a setter is a gun dog with a long, feathery coat

explanation.surface: A rude rant: calling the magazine's puzzle-maker a sodomite and a mangy mongrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' marks bugger as an example: it is a cross word, read as two words. 'Shaggy' also winks at the slang sense of having sex.
explanation.definitionFit: Cyclops is the pseudonym of the setter who compiles Private Eye's puzzle, so the clue points at its own author.

clue.text: Go in for bondage or perverse exercise

definitions.note: a verb phrase standing for a noun: rope is what you would need if you went in for bondage

indicators.note: perverse means contrary, turned the wrong way, so the small word before it is read backwards

blocks.note: taken as written
PE is physical education, school exercise

explanation.surface: Advice to take up kinky sex as an alternative to working out.
explanation.definitionFit: Rope is the cord used to tie someone up, the basic equipment of bondage play.

clue.text: As bloody-minded as Sweeney Todd could get?

blocks.note: first meaning: bad-tempered and obstructive
second meaning, a punning one: a barber sharpens his razor on a leather strop, so he is full of strops

explanation.walkthrough: Sweeney Todd is the murderous barber of Fleet Street. 'Bloody' nods at his killings, and the joke reads the answer as 'covered in razor strops'.
explanation.definitionFit: Stroppy is British informal for bad-tempered and awkward; a strop is a fit of sulking as well as a razor-sharpening strap.

clue.text: Bush ramble: "Statute reversed – UK boat rocked"

indicators.note: reversed means turned back to front, so the legal word is read from right to left
rocked means shaken about, so these letters are jumbled

blocks.note: a statute is a law passed by parliament
taken as written

explanation.surface: A headline-like line that echoes the 2009 film The Boat That Rocked, about pirate radio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bush' suggests George W. Bush, but here it is the Australian outback.
explanation.definitionFit: A walkabout is a journey on foot through the Australian bush, traditionally made by Aboriginal people.

clue.text: An area for curling around the nuts? Ponder afresh!

indicators.note: nuts means crazy, so the short word beside it is jumbled
around means surrounding, so the ice venue goes either side of the jumbled word

blocks.note: curling is played on an ice rink
taken as written

explanation.surface: A crude joke about a place where hair curls around the testicles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nuts' looks like slang for testicles but it is the anagram signal. Curling is a sport sliding stones across ice.
explanation.definitionFit: To rethink is to reconsider a matter from the start, thinking it through again in a new light.

clue.text: Eye's report on Cameron's first meeting with Brenda mishandled: initially a long-range threat

indicators.note: a report is something heard, so the word before it is taken by its sound
the first of a name is its opening letter, so only that one letter is kept
initially means at the start, so each of the two words before it gives only its opening letter

blocks.note: the letter I is pronounced exactly like the word eye
the opening letter of the Prime Minister's surname
the opening letters of these two words

explanation.surface: Private Eye reports that David Cameron botched his first audience with the Queen, nicknamed Brenda by the Eye.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye calls the Queen 'Brenda'. The colon separates the wordplay from the definition at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: An ICBM is an intercontinental ballistic missile, a nuclear weapon threatening targets thousands of miles away.

clue.text: Labour is no longer represented by elected party leader, one with obligation

definitions.note: a fill-in: the answer completes the phrase rather than replacing it

indicators.note: a leader comes at the front, so only the opening letter of the word is used

blocks.note: a candidate who is elected gets in
the opening letter of the word
one who owes something

explanation.surface: Comment after the 2010 election, when Labour lost office, wondering who now speaks for it.
explanation.walkthrough: This puzzle appeared in August 2010, months after Labour lost the general election to the Conservative and Liberal Democrat coalition.
explanation.definitionFit: After losing the 2010 election, Labour was no longer in government, which is what being in power means.

clue.text: Corporation break up produces gutsy glee

blocks.note: corporation is old jocular British slang for a large paunch
to break up is to collapse into laughter

explanation.surface: Splitting up a big company brings bold delight, as a business column might put it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corporation' looks like a company, and 'break up' its dismantling, but both are the comic senses.
explanation.definitionFit: A belly laugh is a deep, hearty laugh from the gut, so 'gutsy glee' describes it with a pun.

clue.text: Balls turned up without a date to make out with

indicators.note: in a down entry, turned up means flipped to read from bottom to top
without means lacking, so those letters are taken out

blocks.note: slang for testicles, which are gonads
taken as written
D is the abbreviation for date

explanation.surface: Someone shows up without a date and needs a partner to fool around with.
explanation.walkthrough: Snog is British slang for kissing passionately.
explanation.definitionFit: To snog someone is to kiss and cuddle them at length, the British word for what Americans call making out.

clue.text: Twisting, liar MPs tossing male off

indicators.note: tossing throws things about, so the letters land in a new order
off means taken away, so the male letter is removed before the shuffle

blocks.note: taken as written
M is the standard abbreviation for male

explanation.surface: Lying MPs are twisting and turning as they throw off one of their number.
explanation.definitionFit: A spiral shape winds round and round, so as an adjective it describes something coiling or turning on itself.

clue.text: Energy-eating explosive European trouser snake formation?

indicators.note: something eating another takes it inside itself, so the energy symbol goes within the explosive

blocks.note: TNT is the explosive trinitrotoluene
E is the physics symbol for energy
a Pole is a native of Poland

explanation.surface: A lurid tabloid line about an explosive European's sexual prowess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trouser snake' is jokey slang for the penis; a tent pole is slang for the erection that raises the bedclothes or trousers like a tent.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang: an erection, the shape a trouser snake takes, is likened to the upright prop holding up a tent.

clue.text: (& 22ac.) Sportingly using other grounds as a basis for divorce proceedings?

blocks.note: first meaning: a team playing a match at the opponents' ground
second meaning: British slang for having an affair

explanation.walkthrough: 'Grounds' hints at legal grounds for divorce while also meaning sports grounds. In British slang a spouse who is unfaithful is said to be playing away.
explanation.definitionFit: The sporting phrase for an away fixture doubles as an idiom for adultery, a traditional reason given for a divorce.

clue.text: Dicky randily embracing love with working Cockney air

indicators.note: dicky is British slang for faulty or unsound, so the letters are rearranged
embracing means holding in the arms, so one letter goes inside the word

blocks.note: taken as written
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O
a machine that is working is on

explanation.surface: A lewd scene of a randy embrace, with a working-class Londoner's tune in the background.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dicky' tempts as slang for the penis, but it is the anagram signal meaning dodgy.
explanation.definitionFit: This 1911 music-hall song is a singalong favourite associated with Cockney Londoners, so it is a Cockney tune.

clue.text: Gaga: "OK, I'm bony, I reckon"

indicators.note: gaga means senile or crazed, so the letters that follow are scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The pop star Lady Gaga admits she thinks herself rather skinny.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gaga' looks like the singer's name speaking, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom expresses a personal opinion, the same as prefacing a view with an admission that this is what one thinks.

clue.text: Tweaked a trail cowboy's dangly thing?

indicators.note: to tweak is to twist and adjust, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Smutty innuendo about a cowboy having his dangly bits tweaked.
explanation.definitionFit: A lariat is a lasso, the long rope a cowboy carries hanging at his saddle, so it is a dangling item.

clue.text: Get knotted? No, carry on as you are

definitions.text: Get knotted? No, carry on as you are

blocks.note: surface reading: a rude British brush-off, like 'get lost'

blocks.clueFragment: No, carry on as you are
blocks.note: setter's reading: 'get knotted' means tie the knot, marry; refusing that and staying as an unwed couple

explanation.walkthrough: 'Get knotted' is British slang for 'go away', but tying the knot is marrying, so the advice is to keep cohabiting unmarried.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes an unmarried couple sharing a home, once thought sinful, the alternative to getting married.

clue.text: Stop senior getting into smack

indicators.note: getting into something means going inside it, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: a senior person is elderly
to smack someone is to strike them

explanation.surface: A shout to halt a pensioner being drawn into heroin, smack being slang for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smack' suggests the drug, heroin, but here it is a blow.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are commands telling someone to halt or wait right now, as an interjection.

clue.text: Ringo: band's last member to get more wacky?

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: the final letter of the word
rum is British informal for odd, so rummer is odder

explanation.surface: Wondering whether Ringo, the Beatles' supposed last recruit, became the band's oddest member.
explanation.definitionFit: Ringo Starr played the drums in the Beatles, so he is an example of a drummer.

clue.text: Drink has Fanny missing a period

indicators.note: missing means lacking, so a letter is dropped from the slang word

blocks.note: both are crude slang for the female genitals
taken as written
an age is a period of history

explanation.surface: A worry that someone called Fanny has missed her menstrual period.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang fanny means the vulva, not the buttocks as in America; beaver is the equivalent slang. Remove its A and add AGE.
explanation.definitionFit: A beverage is any liquid for drinking, so the noun is a synonym for a drink.

clue.text: Strobes: "Me, a rogue, at heart? Slur!"

indicators.note: at heart means in the middle, so the letters sit inside the run of words

blocks.note: the letters run across the words without a break

explanation.surface: A clubber under strobe lights asks whether they are a rogue deep down, slurring drunkenly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slur' looks like drunken speech but it is the verb meaning to smear a reputation.
explanation.definitionFit: To besmear is to smear or soil, figuratively to slander, which is also what a slur does to a name.

clue.text: Just Miliband sorted out?

blocks.note: just means fair, right
Ed Miliband, who became Labour leader in 2010

explanation.surface: Musing whether one of the Miliband brothers simply got sorted out in the 2010 Labour leadership race.
explanation.walkthrough: The Labour leadership contest of 2010 pitted brothers David and Ed Miliband against each other.
explanation.definitionFit: To right a wrong or a capsized boat is to correct it, so righted means put straight or sorted out.

clue.text: E-advertising that's aimed at the end user?

definitions.text: E-advertising that's aimed at the end user?

blocks.note: E is slang for the drug ecstasy
pushing a product is promoting it hard

explanation.surface: Sounds like an online marketing campaign targeting the consumer at the end of the supply chain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'E-' looks like the electronic prefix of e-commerce, but it is ecstasy. The whole clue is also the definition: dealers push drugs to the end user.
explanation.definitionFit: Drug-pushing is selling illegal narcotics, aimed at the addict who consumes them, the 'user' in drug slang.

clue.text: (& 21dn.) Shit dress for a ship's upper location

blocks.note: poop is a childish word for excrement
to deck someone out is to dress them up

explanation.surface: A crude remark that a dress is fit for nothing but the top of a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: The poop deck is the raised deck at the stern of a ship, the highest part of the hull.

clue.text: Given good money, fist a prince

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good
the rand is South Africa's currency
dukes are fists, from rhyming slang

explanation.surface: A bribe offered so that someone will sexually assault a royal, put as crudely as possible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dukes' for fists comes from rhyming slang: Duke of Yorks, forks, i.e. hands.
explanation.definitionFit: A grand duke is a sovereign ruler or royal prince ranking just below a king, as in Luxembourg or imperial Russia.
